CONTRACTS SIGNED BEFORE THE CORPORATION OR LLC EXISTS — PREORGANIZATION CONTRACTS, ADOPTION, AND RATIFICATION (CORP. CODE §§ 200, 17702.01, 25019; CIV. CODE §§ 1530–1532, 1589, 2307–2313, 2342–2343; 02 DEVELOPMENT, LLC V. 607 SOUTH PARK, LLC; EL RIO OILS, LTD. V. PACIFIC COAST ASPHALT CO.; CLEVELAND V. JOHNSON) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Harbor Lane Coffee, LLC · Jordan Lee

PURPOSE AND SCOPE — CONTRACTS MADE BEFORE A CALIFORNIA CORPORATION OR LLC EXISTS
This information sheet concerns an agreement that Jordan Lee signed in the name of Harbor Lane Coffee, LLC with Pat Morgan on March 3, 2026, at a time when Harbor Lane Coffee, LLC had not yet been formed. It describes what California law says about agreements of that kind: the statutes that fix the moment a corporation or a limited liability company begins to exist (Corporations Code sections 200 and 17702.01); the Court of Appeal's statement in 02 Development, LLC v. 607 South Park, LLC that a business entity that does not yet exist is not a party to a contract signed in its name, and its holding that the entity may nonetheless enforce a preorganization contract made on its behalf once it comes into existence and adopts or ratifies it; the older statement of the same rule in El Rio Oils, Ltd. v. Pacific Coast Asphalt Co.; the Civil Code's general rules on ratification, including ratification by accepting or retaining the benefit of an act with notice of it (sections 2307, 2310, 2312, 2313, and 1589); the Court of Appeal's treatment in Cleveland v. Johnson of what evidence supports a later-formed corporation's ratification of a preincorporation contract, including the knowledge that must be shown and the self-dealing limit drawn from Commercial Lumber Co. v. Ukiah Lumber Mills; the Civil Code provisions stating when a person who assumes to act as an agent is responsible to third persons as a principal (sections 2342 and 2343); the Civil Code's definition of novation and the ways a novation is made (sections 1530 through 1532); the fiduciary position California courts have long assigned to promoters; and the inclusion of a "preorganization certificate or subscription" in the statutory definition of a security (Corporations Code section 25019). Whether Harbor Lane Coffee, LLC was in fact formed, when its articles were filed, what the agreement with Pat Morgan says, whether anyone adopted or ratified it, what any party knew, and who is bound by it are all facts this sheet does not determine. Naming the parties and a date here does not establish that any rule described below applies to this agreement, and this sheet states what the statutes and the courts say rather than advising anyone what to do about a particular contract, claim, or defense.

THE MOMENT A CALIFORNIA CORPORATION OR LIMITED LIABILITY COMPANY BEGINS TO EXIST
California fixes the beginning of each entity's existence at a filing with the Secretary of State, not at the moment the people behind it decide to form it. For corporations, Corporations Code section 200(a) says a corporation is formed by executing and filing articles of incorporation, and section 200(c) says that the corporate existence begins upon the filing of the articles. For limited liability companies, Corporations Code section 17702.01(a) says one or more persons act as organizers by signing and delivering articles of organization to the Secretary of State for filing, and section 17702.01(d) says the company is formed when the Secretary of State has filed them. Section 17702.01(e) adds that, except in a proceeding by the state to dissolve the company, the filing is conclusive proof that the organizer satisfied all conditions to formation.

On the face of these sections, the events that often precede a filing — agreeing to go into business together, choosing or reserving a name, signing an operating agreement or a founders' agreement, obtaining a taxpayer identification number, opening a bank account, printing business cards, or beginning to trade under the intended name — are not the events the statutes make decisive. The statutes identify the filing, and only the filing, as the moment the corporation or the limited liability company exists.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "One or more natural persons, partnerships, associations or corporations, domestic or foreign, may form a corporation under this division by executing and filing articles of incorporation."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 200(a) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Corp. Code § 200(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=200.)
  "The corporate existence begins upon the filing of the articles and continues perpetually, unless otherwise expressly provided by law or in the articles."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 200(c) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Corp. Code § 200(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=200.)
  "One or more persons may act as organizers to form a limited liability company by signing and delivering to the Secretary of State for filing articles of organization on a form prescribed by the Secretary of State."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17702.01(a) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Corp. Code § 17702.01(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17702.01.)
  "A limited liability company is formed when the Secretary of State has filed the articles of organization."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17702.01(d) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Corp. Code § 17702.01(d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17702.01.)
  "Except in a proceeding by this state to dissolve a limited liability company, the filing of the articles of organization by the Secretary of State is conclusive proof that the organizer satisfied all conditions to the formation of a limited liability company."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17702.01(e) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Corp. Code § 17702.01(e) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17702.01.)
  Known gap: These two sections state when a corporation and a limited liability company come into existence; neither says anything about the legal effect of agreements made before that moment, which is the subject of the remaining clauses of this sheet. Other California business entities are governed by other statutes not quoted here: a limited partnership is formed under Corporations Code section 15902.01, a registered limited liability partnership under section 16953, and a general partnership can be formed by the conduct of the partners without any filing at all under section 16202 — this corpus addresses those elsewhere. Section 17702.01 was last amended by Stats. 2022, Ch. 617, and section 200 by Stats. 1983, Ch. 1223, as the leginfo text states. Each quoted section was fetched twice from California Legislative Information by two different routes (the single-section view and the whole-chapter or whole-article text view) using different browser identifications, and the quoted sentences matched word for word.

AN ENTITY THAT DOES NOT YET EXIST IS NOT A PARTY TO A CONTRACT SIGNED IN ITS NAME: 02 DEVELOPMENT, LLC V. 607 SOUTH PARK, LLC
In 02 Development, LLC v. 607 South Park, LLC (2008), a person signed an agreement assigning rights in a hotel purchase contract to a limited liability company that had not been organized; he filed the articles of organization about three months later, and the company then sued on the agreement. The seller moved for summary judgment on the ground that there was no enforceable contract with the company because the company did not exist when the assignment agreement was executed, and the trial court granted the motion.

The Court of Appeal reversed. It accepted the premise that a nonexistent business entity cannot be a party to a contract, describing that contention as true but irrelevant, and explained that when the agreement was executed the company did not exist and so was not then a party to it — but that once it came into existence it could enforce a preorganization contract made on its behalf if it adopted or ratified the contract. The distinction the opinion draws is between being a party at the moment of signing, which a nonexistent entity cannot be, and acquiring rights under the agreement afterward by adoption or ratification.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "02 Development did not exist when the parties executed the assignment agreement."
  — 02 Development, LLC v. 607 South Park, LLC, (2008) 159 Cal.App.4th 609, 611 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2303313/02-development-llc-v-607-south-park-llc/)
  "607 South Park’s principal contention to the contrary is that a nonexistent business entity cannot be a party to a contract. The contention is true but irrelevant."
  — 02 Development, LLC v. 607 South Park, LLC, (2008) 159 Cal.App.4th 609, 612 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2303313/02-development-llc-v-607-south-park-llc/)
  "When the assignment agreement was executed, 02 Development did not exist, so it was not then a party to the agreement. But once 02 Development came into existence, it could enforce any preorganization contract made in its behalf, such as the assignment agreement, if it adopted or ratified it."
  — 02 Development, LLC v. 607 South Park, LLC, (2008) 159 Cal.App.4th 609, 612 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2303313/02-development-llc-v-607-south-park-llc/)
  Known gap: This is a Court of Appeal decision (Second Appellate District, Division One) that binds California trial courts under Auto Equity Sales, Inc. v. Superior Court, and no California Supreme Court decision on the point was located. The opinion resolves a summary judgment motion; it decides what the seller's showing failed to establish, not that the company had in fact adopted or ratified the assignment — the court expressly noted that the ratification issue had not been raised in the moving papers, so the burden never shifted on it. The opinion says nothing about the liability of the individual who signed. The text quoted here was fetched twice from CourtListener with two different sets of browser headers, and one quoted phrase was independently confirmed through CourtListener's public search index restricted to this opinion's cluster.

AFTER FORMATION, THE ENTITY MAY ENFORCE A PREORGANIZATION CONTRACT MADE ON ITS BEHALF — AND THE RULE IS THE SAME FOR LLCS
The rule the Court of Appeal applied in 02 Development is an old one in California. In El Rio Oils, Ltd. v. Pacific Coast Asphalt Co. (1949), an oil-sale agreement had been made with two individuals before the defendant corporation was organized; the court described it as a preorganization agreement made for the benefit of the corporation and therefore enforceable by the corporation after its organization, noting that the corporation had adopted and ratified the contract, relied on it, and performed its obligations under it.

02 Development restated the same principle, calling it hornbook law that a corporation can enforce preincorporation contracts made in its behalf and stating that California law does not deviate from that norm. It then addressed the entity type directly: the seller did not argue that limited liability companies should be treated differently from corporations in this respect, and the court said it was aware of no authority supporting such a position. The two decisions together describe adoption or ratification — not the signature itself — as what connects the later-formed entity to the earlier agreement.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]

  — El Rio Oils, Ltd. v. Pacific Coast Asphalt Co., (1949) 95 Cal.App.2d 186, 192 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1162862/el-rio-oils-ltd-v-pacific-coast-asphalt-co/)
  "In the present case the evidence discloses that defendant after its formation as a corporation adopted and ratified the contract, relied upon the agreement, and in all particulars performed the obligation imposed upon it by such agreement."
  — El Rio Oils, Ltd. v. Pacific Coast Asphalt Co., (1949) 95 Cal.App.2d 186, 193 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1162862/el-rio-oils-ltd-v-pacific-coast-asphalt-co/)
  "It is hornbook law that a corporation can enforce preincorporation contracts made in its behalf"
  — 02 Development, LLC v. 607 South Park, LLC, (2008) 159 Cal.App.4th 609, 612 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2303313/02-development-llc-v-607-south-park-llc/)
  "California law does not deviate from that well-established norm."
  — 02 Development, LLC v. 607 South Park, LLC, (2008) 159 Cal.App.4th 609, 612 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2303313/02-development-llc-v-607-south-park-llc/)
  "607 South Park does not argue that limited liability companies should be treated differently from corporations in this respect, and we are aware of no authority that would support such a position."
  — 02 Development, LLC v. 607 South Park, LLC, (2008) 159 Cal.App.4th 609, 612 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2303313/02-development-llc-v-607-south-park-llc/)
  Known gap: El Rio Oils and 02 Development are both Court of Appeal decisions; no California Supreme Court holding on preorganization contracts was located. Both opinions concern a later-formed entity seeking to enforce an agreement, so they state what an entity may do, not what its counterparty may do, and neither decides when adoption or ratification has occurred on contested facts. 02 Development's statement about limited liability companies rests on the absence of contrary authority and on the point not being argued, which the opinion says expressly. The El Rio Oils text on CourtListener is derived from a scanned source and contains optical-character-recognition artifacts elsewhere in the opinion; the sentences quoted here were confirmed word for word in two fetches made with different browser header sets, and one of them was independently confirmed through CourtListener's public search index restricted to this opinion's cluster.

HOW THE CIVIL CODE DESCRIBES RATIFICATION: SUBSEQUENT AUTHORIZATION, ACCEPTANCE OF THE BENEFIT, AND THE POWER TO RATIFY
Adoption and ratification are not defined in the Corporations Code sections that create corporations and limited liability companies; the general rules appear in the Civil Code's agency and contract provisions. Section 2307 says an agency may be created, and an authority conferred, by a precedent authorization or a subsequent ratification. Section 2310 says a ratification can be made only in the manner that would have been necessary to confer the original authority, or, where an oral authorization would suffice, by accepting or retaining the benefit of the act with notice of it. Section 2312 says a ratification is not valid unless, at the time of ratifying, the principal has power to confer authority for the act. Section 2313 says no unauthorized act can be made valid retroactively to the prejudice of third persons without their consent. Outside the agency title, Civil Code section 1589 says a voluntary acceptance of the benefit of a transaction is equivalent to consent to all the obligations arising from it, so far as the facts are known, or ought to be known, to the person accepting.

Read together, these sections describe ratification as something done after the act, by a principal that has the power to authorize the act at the time it ratifies, and capable of being shown by accepting or retaining the benefit with notice — the same route the Court of Appeal followed in the corporate setting in the clause that follows.

Whether section 2310's writing requirement applies to a particular ratification depends on whether the underlying act was one that required written authority, a question these sections answer only by reference to other law. Section 2313's protection of third persons and section 2312's requirement that the principal have the power to confer authority at the time of ratifying are quoted here as the Civil Code states them; no case applying section 2312 to an entity formed after the act was located in this research, though Cleveland v. Johnson, quoted in the next clause, applied section 2310 to a corporation's ratification of a preincorporation contract. Each section was fetched twice from California Legislative Information by two different routes with different browser identifications.

WHAT SUPPORTS A FINDING THAT THE NEW ENTITY RATIFIED: KNOWLEDGE, BENEFIT, AND THE SELF-DEALING LIMIT IN CLEVELAND V. JOHNSON
In Cleveland v. Johnson (2012), an investor put seed money into an internet business operated by an existing corporation under a 1995 agreement; the business was later moved into a new corporation formed in 1996, and a jury found that the new corporation had ratified the preincorporation contract. On appeal the defendants argued there was no substantial evidence of ratification because the new corporation had not known of the old agreement: only the interested directors knew of it, and under Commercial Lumber Co. v. Ukiah Lumber Mills (1949) ratification will not be presumed unless the corporation had actual knowledge of the specific contract out of which the benefits arose, with the knowledge of a director directly interested in the contract, or of a promoter who later becomes a director, not imputed to the corporation.

The Court of Appeal declined to apply that principle on these facts, saying the case did not involve the sort of self-dealing present in Commercial Lumber and that applying it there would eviscerate the principle of ratification. It described the circumstances as virtually mandating recognition that the new corporation ratified the agreement, quoting Civil Code section 2310's acceptance-or-retention-of-benefit route, observing that there could be no dispute that the new corporation benefitted from the investment, and noting that three of its four directors and the lawyer for both corporations had notice of the arrangement. The opinion therefore illustrates both sides of the question: a knowledge requirement drawn from Commercial Lumber, and a self-dealing limit on that requirement.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]

  — Cleveland v. Johnson, (2012) 209 Cal.App.4th 1315, 1335 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5811374/cleveland-v-johnson/)
  "ratification will not be presumed unless the corporation had actual knowledge of the specific contract out of which the benefits arose"

  — Cleveland v. Johnson (quoting Commercial Lumber Co. v. Ukiah Lumber Mills (1949) 94 Cal.App.2d 215, 220-221), (2012) 209 Cal.App.4th 1315, 1335-1336 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5811374/cleveland-v-johnson/)
  "We decline to apply the Commercial Lumber principle on the facts of this case, because this case does not involve the sort of self-dealing that appears in Commercial Lumber, and indeed its application here would eviscerate the principle of ratification."
  — Cleveland v. Johnson, (2012) 209 Cal.App.4th 1315, 1335 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5811374/cleveland-v-johnson/)
  "On the contrary, the circumstances here virtually mandate a recognition that IS West ratified the Cleveland agreement."
  — Cleveland v. Johnson, (2012) 209 Cal.App.4th 1315, 1336 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5811374/cleveland-v-johnson/)

  — Cleveland v. Johnson, (2012) 209 Cal.App.4th 1315, 1336-1337 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5811374/cleveland-v-johnson/)
  Known gap: Cleveland v. Johnson is a Court of Appeal decision (Fourth Appellate District, Division Three) reviewing a jury verdict for substantial evidence; it holds that the evidence supported ratification on those facts, not that any particular set of facts is required. Its treatment of Commercial Lumber is a refusal to apply that decision's language to a case without self-dealing, not a disapproval of it — Commercial Lumber itself is a 1949 Court of Appeal decision that was not independently fetched in this research, and the two sentences attributed to it here are quoted as they appear inside the Cleveland opinion. The CourtListener text of Cleveland is derived from a scanned source and contains optical-character-recognition defects elsewhere in the opinion (for example "[Ejven" for "[E]ven" at the start of the Commercial Lumber passage and "eases" for "cases"); the sentences quoted here were chosen to fall outside those defects and were confirmed word for word in two fetches with different browser header sets. A third, phrase-level confirmation through CourtListener's public search index, restricted to this opinion's cluster, matched the sentence about eviscerating the principle of ratification (that check returned HTTP 429 rate-limit responses on two earlier attempts and succeeded on a later retry).

THE CIVIL CODE PROVISIONS ADDRESSING A PERSON WHO SIGNS AS AGENT FOR A PRINCIPAL THAT DOES NOT EXIST
The decisions quoted above describe what the later-formed entity may do; they say nothing about the individual who signed. The Civil Code addresses a person who assumes to act as an agent in two sections of the agency title. Section 2342 says that one who assumes to act as an agent warrants, to all who deal with that person in that capacity, that he or she has the authority assumed. Section 2343 says that one who assumes to act as an agent is responsible to third persons as a principal for acts in the course of the agency in three listed cases, and in no others: where credit is given to the agent personally with the agent's consent; where the agent enters into a written contract in the name of the principal without believing in good faith that he or she has authority to do so; and where the agent's acts are wrongful in their nature.

Section 2313 supplies a further boundary on the ratification route described above: no unauthorized act can be made valid, retroactively, to the prejudice of third persons, without their consent. Nothing in the Corporations Code sections quoted in this sheet, and nothing in the three decisions quoted in it, states that filing articles later removes an obligation a person took on in his or her own name before the filing.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]

  — Cal. Civ. Code § 2342 (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Civ. Code § 2342 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=2342.)
  "One who assumes to act as an agent is responsible to third persons as a principal for his acts in the course of his agency, in any of the following cases, and in no others: 1. When, with his consent, credit is given to him personally in a transaction; 2. When he enters into a written contract in the name of his principal, without believing, in good faith, that he has authority to do so; or, 3. When his acts are wrongful in their nature."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 2343 (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Civ. Code § 2343 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=2343.)
  "No unauthorized act can be made valid, retroactively, to the prejudice of third persons, without their consent."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 2313 (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Civ. Code § 2313 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=2313.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes the Civil Code's agency provisions and does not state the broader promoter-liability rule found in treatises — that a promoter who contracts for a corporation not yet formed is personally liable on the contract and remains so after the corporation adopts it unless the other party agrees to a novation. Research for this sheet did not locate a published California appellate decision squarely so holding in the sources available here (CourtListener's free full-text search of California Supreme Court and Court of Appeal opinions was searched for the relevant phrases and returned no such decision), and no such rule is stated here on the strength of secondary sources. Sections 2342 and 2343 are general agency provisions written in terms of an agent and a principal; whether and how they apply where the named principal did not exist at all is a question the sections themselves do not answer, and no case applying them to that situation was located. Each quoted section was fetched twice from California Legislative Information by two different routes with different browser identifications. This corpus's sheets on alter ego liability and on the personal tort liability of officers, directors, and members address separate questions.

SUBSTITUTING THE NEW ENTITY FOR THE PERSON WHO SIGNED: WHAT THE CIVIL CODE CALLS A NOVATION
California's statutory mechanism for replacing one obligor with another is novation. Civil Code section 1530 defines novation as the substitution of a new obligation for an existing one. Section 1531 lists the three ways a novation is made: by substituting a new obligation between the same parties with intent to extinguish the old obligation; by substituting a new debtor in place of the old one, with intent to release the latter; or by substituting a new creditor in place of the old one, with intent to transfer the rights of the latter to the former. Section 1532 says a novation is made by contract and is subject to all the rules concerning contracts in general.

The second listed form — substitution of a new debtor in place of the old one, with intent to release the latter — is the one that describes replacing a person who signed with the entity formed afterward. Because section 1532 makes a novation a contract, the rules that govern contracts generally, including the requirement of the parties' consent, apply to it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "Novation is the substitution of a new obligation for an existing one."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1530 (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Civ. Code § 1530 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1530.)
  "Novation is made: 1. By the substitution of a new obligation between the same parties, with intent to extinguish the old obligation; 2. By the substitution of a new debtor in place of the old one, with intent to release the latter; or, 3. By the substitution of a new creditor in place of the old one, with intent to transfer the rights of the latter to the former."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1531 (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Civ. Code § 1531 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1531.)

This clause does not state that a novation is required for any particular result, because the promoter-liability premise that would make that statement meaningful is not established by any California holding located in this research (see the preceding clause's note). No case applying sections 1530 through 1532 to the substitution of a newly formed corporation or limited liability company for the person who signed on its behalf was located. Each section was fetched twice from California Legislative Information by two different routes with different browser identifications.

THE FIDUCIARY POSITION CALIFORNIA COURTS ASSIGN TO PROMOTERS
California decisions have long treated the people who organize a business and raise money for it before it exists — promoters — as occupying a position of trust toward those they bring in. Cleveland v. Johnson quoted the California Supreme Court's statement in California-Calaveras Mining Co. v. Walls (1915) that promoters occupy a position of trust and confidence and that it devolves upon them to make full disclosure.

Applying that principle, the Court of Appeal in Cleveland held that on the facts before it there was substantial evidence that the promoter and the corporation, acting through him as a director, owed a fiduciary duty to the person who had provided the seed money, even though he never received stock: his position was, in the court's view, indistinguishable in any pertinent way from that of a stockholder, since he had provided the seed money and was entitled by contract to share in the profits.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "It is, therefore, clear on principle that promoters, under the circumstances just stated, do occupy a position of trust and confidence, and it devolves upon them to make full disclosure."
  — Cleveland v. Johnson (quoting California-Calaveras Mining Co. v. Walls (1915) 170 Cal. 285, 296), (2012) 209 Cal.App.4th 1315, 1339 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5811374/cleveland-v-johnson/)
  "We disagree, both on the facts and on the law, and hold that in this case, there was substantial evidence that the promoter (Johnson) and the corporation (IS West, acting through Johnson as a director) owed a fiduciary duty to Cleveland as an investor."
  — Cleveland v. Johnson, (2012) 209 Cal.App.4th 1315, 1342 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5811374/cleveland-v-johnson/)
  Known gap: The quoted passage from California-Calaveras Mining Co. v. Walls is reproduced as it appears inside the Cleveland opinion; the 1915 Supreme Court opinion itself was not independently fetched in this research, so the quotation is verified only as Cleveland's text of it. Cleveland is a substantial-evidence review of a jury verdict, and the court stated its holding as one about this case; the accompanying limitation the court placed on that holding is quoted in the final clause of this sheet. The knowledge that a promoter is a fiduciary does not by itself say what disclosure any particular relationship requires, and this sheet does not address the separate fiduciary duties of directors, officers, controlling shareholders, or managers, which other documents in this corpus cover. The Cleveland text on CourtListener is derived from a scanned source with optical-character-recognition defects elsewhere in the opinion; the sentences quoted here were confirmed word for word in two fetches with different browser header sets, and the promoter-fiduciary sentence quoted here was additionally confirmed through CourtListener's public search index, restricted to this opinion's cluster.

MONEY RAISED BEFORE THE ENTITY EXISTS: "PREORGANIZATION CERTIFICATE OR SUBSCRIPTION" IS INSIDE THE STATUTORY DEFINITION OF A SECURITY
California's Corporate Securities Law of 1968 defines the term "security" in Corporations Code section 25019, and the list in that section expressly includes a preorganization certificate or subscription, alongside notes, stock, evidences of indebtedness, certificates of interest or participation in a profit-sharing agreement, and investment contracts. The section adds that all of the listed items are securities whether or not evidenced by a written document.

The practical significance of the definition is that the securities statutes attach to an instrument by what it is, not by whether the entity issuing it has been formed or whether anything was written down.

California fixes the beginning of each entity's existence at a filing with the Secretary of State, not at the moment the people behind it decide to form it. Adoption and ratification are not defined in the Corporations Code sections that create corporations and limited liability companies; the general rules appear in the Civil Code's agency and contract provisions. Section 2307 says an agency may be created, and an authority conferred, by a precedent authorization or a subsequent ratification. Section 2310 says a ratification can be made only in the manner that would have been necessary to confer the original authority, or, where an oral authorization would suffice, by accepting or retaining the benefit of the act with notice of it. Section 2312 says a ratification is not valid unless, at the time of ratifying, the principal has power to confer authority for the act. Section 2313 says no unauthorized act can be made valid retroactively to the prejudice of third persons without their consent. In Cleveland v. Johnson (2012), an investor put seed money into an internet business operated by an existing corporation under a 1995 agreement; the business was later moved into a new corporation formed in 1996, and a jury found that the new corporation had ratified the preincorporation contract. On appeal the defendants argued there was no substantial evidence of ratification because the new corporation had not known of the old agreement: only the interested directors knew of it, and under Commercial Lumber Co. v. Ukiah Lumber Mills (1949) ratification will not be presumed unless the corporation had actual knowledge of the specific contract out of which the benefits arose, with the knowledge of a director directly interested in the contract, or of a promoter who later becomes a director, not imputed to the corporation.

The Court of Appeal declined to apply that principle on these facts, saying the case did not involve the sort of self-dealing present in Commercial Lumber and that applying it there would eviscerate the principle of ratification. It described the circumstances as virtually mandating recognition that the new corporation ratified the agreement, quoting Civil Code section 2310's acceptance-or-retention-of-benefit route, observing that there could be no dispute that the new corporation benefitted from the investment, and noting that three of its four directors and the lawyer for both corporations had notice of the arrangement. The opinion therefore illustrates both sides of the question: a knowledge requirement drawn from Commercial Lumber, and a self-dealing limit on that requirement.

California's statutory mechanism for replacing one obligor with another is novation. Civil Code section 1530 defines novation as the substitution of a new obligation for an existing one. Section 1531 lists the three ways a novation is made: by substituting a new obligation between the same parties with intent to extinguish the old obligation; by substituting a new debtor in place of the old one, with intent to release the latter; or by substituting a new creditor in place of the old one, with intent to transfer the rights of the latter to the former. Section 1532 says a novation is made by contract and is subject to all the rules concerning contracts in general.

The second listed form — substitution of a new debtor in place of the old one, with intent to release the latter — is the one that describes replacing a person who signed with the entity formed afterward. Because section 1532 makes a novation a contract, the rules that govern contracts generally, including the requirement of the parties' consent, apply to it.

Both Court of Appeal decisions quoted in this sheet limited what they were deciding, and the limits are on the face of the opinions. In 02 Development, the seller argued on appeal that there was no evidence the company ratified the assignment agreement after it came into existence; the court did not reach that question, because the point had not been raised in the moving papers below, so the burden of production never shifted and the asserted absence of evidence was not a ground for affirming. The decision therefore establishes that a nonexistent entity's later formation does not by itself defeat the contract, not that ratification occurred.

In Cleveland, the court, immediately after holding that the promoter and the corporation owed a fiduciary duty to the investor before it, said that it was not saying that all corporations or promoters owe fiduciary duties to all investors under all circumstances. Neither opinion addresses who else may be bound by a contract signed before the entity existed, what happens if the entity is never formed, or what a counterparty may do.

citations.case: 02 Development, LLC v. 607 South Park, LLC
citations.quote: Consequently, the burden of production never shifted to 02 Development to present evidence of ratification, so the alleged absence of such evidence does not constitute a ground for affirmance.

citations.case: Cleveland v. Johnson
citations.quote: We do not say that, under all circumstances, all corporations or promoters owe fiduciary duties to all “investors.”

expectedJSON.gap: This clause states the boundaries the two opinions placed on themselves; it is not a list of every issue they left open, and it is not a statement that any other rule applies. Questions this sheet does not reach include the effect of the statute of frauds on an agreement signed in the name of an entity that did not exist, the treatment of entities other than corporations and limited liability companies, the treatment of a foreign corporation or foreign limited liability company that had not yet registered in California, whether an agreement was ever adopted or ratified on particular facts, and the tax consequences of pre-formation expenditures. The quoted sentences were confirmed word for word in two fetches of each opinion made with different browser header sets; for 02 Development a phrase was also confirmed through CourtListener's public search index restricted to that opinion's cluster, and for Cleveland two other sentences from the same opinion were confirmed the same way after earlier rate-limited attempts.

Executed on January 1, 2026 at Los Angeles, California.

[This information sheet describes California Corporations Code sections 200, 17702.01, and 25019, California Civil Code sections 1530 through 1532, 1589, 2307, 2310, 2312, 2313, 2342, and 2343, and the decisions in 02 Development, LLC v. 607 South Park, LLC (2008) 159 Cal.App.4th 609, El Rio Oils, Ltd. v. Pacific Coast Asphalt Co. (1949) 95 Cal.App.2d 186, and Cleveland v. Johnson (2012) 209 Cal.App.4th 1315. It is educational only. It does not determine whether Harbor Lane Coffee, LLC was formed, whether the agreement of March 3, 2026 was made on its behalf, whether anyone adopted or ratified it, whether Jordan Lee or Harbor Lane Coffee, LLC owes anything to Pat Morgan, or whether any arrangement described in it is a security. Whether a preorganization contract has been adopted or ratified, and who is bound by it, is a determination made by a court applying the statutes and case law to the specific facts presented.]
